utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances please. But before I do that, I note for the record that we reconvene under Rule 15 bis, Judge Harhoff being involved in another matter that is concurrently sitting with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis, along with Belinda Pidwell and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is no reason to delay us, would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And Aleksandar Aleksic who has just appeared in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Bajagic. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, yesterday towards the very end of the session we discussed paragraphs 145, 146, and 147 in relation to Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs. Tab 32, footnote 42.3 [as interpreted]. P530 is its number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Law on Internal Affairs on our monitors, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, can I get those binders with the tabs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I apologise. Thank you for having reminded me. P530. So Exhibit 530, tab 32, footnote 142.3. We need Article 27 and 32. That is page 4 in the Serbian text and I think it is page 4 and 5 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, yesterday on page 20145, -146, and -147, you spoke about these matters. You do recall that we mentioned some examples in terms of regulations of municipal authorities that were according to the law submitted to the Ministry of the Interior. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you explained to us then, and we also showed that on different examples, what kind of regulations this involved; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since I have demonstrated the context, I would like to show a few documents that I would like you to comment upon. I would like you to say a few words about the nature of these documents. Tab 16. 65 ter Defence 626D1. Let us just wait for the English translation. We see it now. Mr. Bajagic, this is a document of the local organ of government from that time, the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most. The date is the 31st of May, 1992. The form is that of an order. And we see that it was also submitted to the public security station. We see that under number 3. Bearing in mind everything that we discussed beforehand, the provisions of the law, can you give us your comment regarding the nature of this document? When I say the nature of this document, I mean from the point of view of the Ministry of the Interior and its functioning.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, as we can see, is an order that the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, therefore an executive organ, is sending to several institutions. It cannot be one of the examples that we've already demonstrated in relation to Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs because this does not involve sending a document that involves an initiative or a proposal regarding a certain problem. This, rather, is a direct order from a municipal organ of government to various entities, including the public security station, that should act in accordance with that order. So we are not looking at it in the context of Article 27 of the law; rather, this is an order issued by the Crisis Staff to the public security station as the lowest-ranking organ in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in your view, this kind of order of a local organ of government to the local public security station, is that in accordance with the law or has that kind of situation been envisaged by the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such orders are not in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs and not with -- they are not in accordance with other laws that were in force at the time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, public security stations or organs, do they have a duty based on the law and regulations pertaining to Internal Affairs? Do they have to act in accordance with such orders?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Public security stations and other organisations on a territorial basis do not have the duty to act in accordance with such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 146 and the footnote pertaining to that paragraph, and that is footnote 179, you list a number of documents by way of an illustration to the effect that such orders were implemented directly after all.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are documents that I have singled out of a large body of documents that I researched in order to illustrate my previously presented position. As for all of these documents listed in 179, they show that the local government organs, that is to say at municipal levels and higher, issued orders to organi units of the Ministry of the Interior, and in one of these documents, they were exactly -- actually dealing with personnel matters, which is in direct contravention of the Law on the Ministry -- on Internal Affairs. As we can see, these are the last two documents that are listed here; its decision on the appointment of commanders in the Prijedor SJB and the decision on the appointment of the commander of the Omarska SJB. Actually, such decisions made by Crisis Staffs as municipal executive organs are absolutely not in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serb Republic of BH that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us what was in accordance with the law. Can you explain that briefly, the procedure involved?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the law, these appointments can be made by the head of the centre of security stations with the agreement of the ministry headquarters, and it meant that there should be accompanying documents, namely clearance related to the candidate, and other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In these two cases, did you have any -- any parameters that would indicate that the chief of the CSB was aware of this, of these orders or, rather, decisions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I analyse these two documents that we are speaking about specifically, nowhere can we see from these documents that the chief of the CSB that involved the territory of these two public security stations was aware of the appointment of these persons or that he gave his consent. These two documents clearly show that it was only the municipal organs of government that carried out this appointment. Once again, I say that it is not in accordance with the law that was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do have an initial objection. The last two documents spoken about, I believe, are 65 ter 0084D1 and 0107D1; is that correct? The two Prijedor appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the reference. I have the reference in the footnotes. Footnote 179.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm looking at that. Is that the appointment of the commanders in Prijedor SJB and the appointment of commander for Omarska SJB?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The footnote lists those both as being dated 11 May 1992, at least in my English translation of the report. And the documents themselves in e-court seem to be 11 May 1993. And therefore if they're May 1993, I object as they're outside the scope of our indictment period, and therefore I think they're not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But there is a misunderstanding. I will check in the original, also it says 1992. And I will check these documents during the break, and I'll come back to that. What I was offering --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've looked at the originals in e-court and they do say 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hannis, I tendered the document from tab 16. 626D1 is its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's the document regarding Sanski Most Crisis Staff, I don't have an objection to that. But I understood you to be talking now about footnote 179 and the appointments of the chief for Prijedor SJB and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was making -- I'm sorry, I need to explain. I showed this document to the witness, the witness commented on the document, then I was making a relation between this document and the number of documents listed in his footnote 179. And then the witness mentioned these two documents and we continued talking about that. But what I'm offering is this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection to the Sanski Most document. Only to note, Your Honours, that it is a document that appears the Defence had at the beginning of the Prosecution case and could have and should have been shown to one of the Sanski Most witnesses who testified here in the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. No doubt that last point, Mr. Hannis, will be the subject of a Prosecution submission much later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 626D1 will become Exhibit 1D536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are you through with this line of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is a question by way of clarification which I wish to put to the witness, and it is this: And here I'm going to rely heavily on the assistance of the interpreters to convey the concepts that I'm trying to separate. And it is this: I'm familiar from my own experiences and I'm sure is isn't peculiar to my country, it's probably universal, that decisions such as appointments like this could be irregular but nevertheless valid. Do I understand, Mr. Bajagic, that you are saying that these appointments were merely irregular or that they were wholly invalid or illegal? Do you understand the distinction I'm making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't specific. These appointments were not in accordance with the law, so they were unlawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But could they, notwithstanding that they were unlawful, in your view be effective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course such unlawful appointments have an effect. They simply show that the Ministry of the Interior could not establish a single chain of running that organ. Of course, proposals and initiatives regarding certain candidates could come from municipal organs of government, but they cannot authoritatively make appointments by way of their own decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could my volume please be turned down? It is very disconcerting. It's too loud. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear well now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear now? Now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you but it's very loud. I can hear this echo. It's okay. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again it's loud, but never mind; I don't want to make a problem. Obviously not much can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, when you answered His Honour's questions, the questions put by Judge Hall, the honourable presiding judge, you said that that was not in accordance with the law. Which law did you have in mind when you said that, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic, while preparing this expert report, did you come across any other situations in which such decisions or similar ones made by local government organs were made and sent to public security stations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The examples I referred to in footnote 179 of my expert report are but a few documents in relation to the sea of documents that I found when writing this expert report. I would like to draw your attention to footnotes in other parts of the report that also indicate that municipal government organs very often with regard to different questions issued immediate directions and orders to public security stations. As in the case of the documents from footnote 179, that is not in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serb Republic of BH which was passed in 1992, as we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that you are actually saying that this was the de facto situation? Is this understanding of mine correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part of my expert report I analysed the de facto situation on the ground with regard to the organisation and the functioning of the MUP. All I have previously said is -- has to do with this situation: The relations that existed between the ministry and the individual organisational units in the territory of the Serb Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the following document, tab 15, 65 ter 614D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I'm going to show you another document, one that is not cited in the footnotes of your expert report. This is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality signed by its president, Dr. Stakic, and it's about the method of calculation and payment of salaries in enterprises, organisation, and communities for the month of May. Here's what I would like to know: If you have any comment about this document, especially paragraph 2 of item 4 of this document, then I would like to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks for scrolling, or, rather, turning the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is one of those I spoke about. This is about the payment of salaries pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality. These salaries are also those of the members of the SJB. This activity of the municipal authorities is also not in compliance with the Law on Home Affairs [as interpreted] because the MUP, as a centralised body of public administration, had a unified manner of paying salaries internally, from the top down to the lowest organisational unit. Members of the MUP, by virtue of taking up employment with the ministry, were entitled to receive salaries under the law in this unified manner. Although it is not a bad thing that the municipal authorities should take care of persons too, but still this is not in compliance with the law, because municipal authorities, without any previous agreement, are not entitled to pay salaries or nor do they have the right to request certificates, as we see in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic, do you know which local authorities in 1992 in the territory of the RS or, more broadly speaking, in Bosnia-Herzegovina were created, and possibly if you know the sequence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the level of local authorities in that system there were Municipal Assemblies and their Executive Boards as their, well, executive bodies. And the system that prevailed in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the beginning, that is, April, Crisis Staffs began emerging. But then pursuant to a decision of the highest authorities of the state, they were transformed into War Presidencies. Finally, which means in late June, I believe, but let me not speculate - you can find exact information in my expert report - these War Presidencies, also pursuant to a decision of the highest authorities of the state, became war commissions. Such names of these local authorities were finally abolished by decisions of the highest state authorities, and what existed later on were Executive Boards. That's what I can say about that level of authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it -- about the payment of salaries by the municipality authorities rather than by the ministry, is it -- would it be in your line of question to ask why they did so? Why the municipalities did pay salaries? Where normally I would say it's not a natural thing to do, for authorities to pay things they don't have to pay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You are going to ask that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, please tell me, when you said Executive Boards, did you mean the Executive Boards as the executive bodies of the Municipal Assemblies or something else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the executive bodies of the Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You heard the question of His Honour Judge Delvoie. What, in your opinion or as a result of your survey, was the reason for the fact that the salaries for members of the SJBs were paid by local authorities rather than the central authorities, as it should be under the law, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without going into everything that characterises the functioning of the MUP of the Serb Republic in 1992, it was not only the matter of salaries, but many other matters concerning the functioning of SJBs. The executive bodies of the municipalities tried to deal with them, which, as I said, is not in compliance with the Law on Home Affairs. My conclusion is that the municipal authorities tried to exert influence, unlawful and unconstitutional influence, on SJBs and other local authorities. In other words, Crisis Staffs at municipal level tried to influence the work of the SJBs to a very high extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I just intervene. Regarding the transcript at page 12, line 24, it's translated as: "... is not in compliance with the Law on Home Affairs." I wonder if that was meant to be "Internal Affairs" because that's the term we've always been using. And I want to be sure there's not some other law about home affairs that we haven't heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. What the witness says was Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But then, Mr. Bajagic, if this is some sort of conflict between the municipal and territorial or the state level, I would expect that the ministry would also pay the salaries and that the people would have been paid two times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Or, rather, I didn't deal with the matter of paying out salaries to members of the MUP separately. I didn't focus on that topic in my expert report. But if we are talking about this, we must bear in mind the territorial fragmentation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. Very often, especially in the first six months, it was impossible to have communication even by courier between the ministry and the -- all the territorial units, from the CSBs down to the SJBs and police stations. In such a situation, to my mind, there should again be some way of exchanging information about that or some sort of approval of the ministry to the Executive Boards to pay salaries. We don't see Mr. Stakic referring to any sort of communication with the MUP, possibly making a proposal or launching an initiative, which would be his right under Article 27 of the law. But instead, the Executive Board passed this decision independently, without consulting anyone. This is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But then the basic situation was that without the municipality taking care of it, people wouldn't have been paid, which makes the situation, rather than a conflict between the central and the regional level, another kind of situation by which the municipality took care of something the ministry couldn't take care of. And wouldn't that mean that they must have been communicating somehow to know whether the salaries were paid or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that anybody received double salaries at the time, both from the municipal bodies and from the ministry. I suppose, with a high degree of certainty, that all employees did receive salaries but possibly with some delay on the ground. I haven't found a document stating that anybody received their salary from two sources. The MUP certainly took care of its members, the MUP headquarters, I mean. But for these very problems, the salaries arrived at the lowest organisational level with delay. That's what I can offer by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you mentioned the establishment of war-time commissions. I'll show you a document from tab 5, 65 ter 443D1.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, could you repeat which tab it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see Radovan Karadzic's name in the signature block; he was president of the Presidency. The document is dated 10 June. On page 1, we saw that it's a decision about the establishment of war-time commissions in municipalities during the imminent threat of war or the state of war. Could you please comment Article 2 briefly, then Articles 5 and 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having spoken about the names of the executive authorities in the municipalities of the Serb Republic of BH as of the beginning of the war and the introduction of the state of the imminent threat of war, I said that they were first called Crisis Staffs, then War Presidencies and finally war commissions. This is a decision, and its a document signed by the president of the Presidency, Radovan Karadzic, on the 10th of June, 1992. It's a decision on the establishment of war commissions in the municipalities of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the level of each municipality, as we see in Article 2, they shall consist of a state commissioner and four members from the ranks of the most influential citizens within the Crisis Staff, the economy, and the ruling party. Article 5 of this document reads: "On the day when the war commissions are constituted, they will supersede Crisis Staffs ..." And Article 6 of this decision, could we please see it? The decision on the establishment of War Presidencies is abolished. That decision was adopted on 31 May. Which means that only ten days later, ten days after the decision to establish War Presidencies, this decision to abolish both the Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies was taken, and it was decided to establish war commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, if you know, whether in the former organs of authority, territorial organs, republican commissioners were involved in them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry about that. As for the Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies, did they include the republican commissioner as well?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies functioned only at the level of local government. There were only representatives of the local government there. It's only from the 10th of June onwards, when the decision was made to establish war commissioners from the republican level, it was envisaged to send commissioners who would, together with those most prominent members at local level, the four of them, would exercise executive authority in a municipality, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document in this form is not an exhibit yet. We have a version of this document with an identical text, I must say, in our law library and it is L65. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber believes it is necessary to have this document admitted as well because it has a seal and the signature of the president of the Presidency. I leave the matter to the Trial Chamber, whatever you deem appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you assist me, Mr. Zecevic. When you say the document with the identical text is in the law library, what's the difference between -- was there a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's -- it was -- it is in the law library because it has been printed in the Official Gazette. That is the only reason. This is the original decision, and what we have in the law library is a reprint of that decision in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's just what I was going to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I was going so say. L65 is the newspaper edition of the Official Gazette version of the same document. I have no objection. The contents are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know that we need both. We have it in the law library already. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we need both; I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- trying to get the assistance from the Trial Chamber. And, of course, the other position of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I'm going to show you the next document. That is tab 12; 65 ter number is 474D1. Mr. Bajagic, this is another document that is not referred to in the footnotes of your report, but I have most certainly shown it to you during your proofing and you are familiar with the document. These are minutes from a joint session of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 1st of July, and we see who the attendees are: The president of the Presidency is there, the speaker of the Assembly, the prime minister, and some ministers as well. What I am particularly interested in is page 5, the last paragraph. I would like to hear your comment, if any, with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, it is the paragraph that starts with the words [B/C/S spoken], "furthermore," "in addition to that." Bearing in mind what is mentioned here as a conclusion, it is stated that the members of the Presidency and the Government of the Serb Republic of BH --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honour, may I intervene at this moment. I just want to indicate that I have an objection to the witness commenting on this particular document. It's the minutes -- purported to be the minutes of a joint meeting of the government and the Presidency. However, there's no stamp, there's no number at the beginning of this document. There's no seal. It's typewritten. I'm not sure if it's complete or official. In addition, this witness is a police expert, and the subject matter of this paragraph does not appear to pertain to police matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, a number of -- Office of the Prosecutor already admitted exhibits as well as some of Defence exhibits already admitted in this case which are the minutes of the meetings of the Presidency, of the extended Presidency, of the government, or the joint meetings between the Presidency and the government have been already admitted. None of them has any signature or any stamp, which is only normal because it's the -- it's the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we deal with the second part of the objection first which may make the first part irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Your Honours, the witness commented, and I can give a reference if you would bear with me, but maybe you will recall when I explain. The witness explained in his expert report the situation about -- and yesterday, as a matter of fact, during the -- at the very end of his testimony -- end of session yesterday, about the fact that there has been two particular periods in 1992 concerning the constitutional settings of Republika Srpska. Namely, the first period until September 1992 and then the amendments to the constitution have been introduced and then the situation changed as so-called, let's call it the second period. Now, this paragraph over here directly talks about this -- about these facts, and that is why I think that the witness can give comment on this, Your Honours, because it's a part of his expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but I could see the argument about the document itself. What I am not clear on, and I think that this is what I understand Mr. Hannis' intervention to be, what makes the witness who is at present on the stand any more competent to comment on this than anybody else picking up the document and reading it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition, Your Honour, my additional objection is that this is a document that should have been shown to Dr. Djeric, Milan Trbojevic, or Momcilo Mandic, who are all listed as being present at this meeting and you who have all been here and testified in this case. And as far as I know, it was not shown to any of those three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really have a problem with this objection. First of all, if I had this document, I would have surely shown it to these witnesses which Mr. Hannis has mentioned. Of course. There is no -- there should be no doubt why should I be withholding the document which is actually in my favour from the Office of the Prosecutor or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I don't know that we need a response to that particular objection, because again, as with an earlier observation that Mr. Hannis made, this is a matter for argument at some later stage. So I don't know that you need to respond specifically to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I come back to the question of the document in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the only nexus I see between this witness and this document is the fact that the witness, as expert, talks in his report, and I can -- if you bear with me two more minutes, I will give you the specific references in his expert report where he talks about this specific situation in the Republika Srpska in the context which, according to the witness and his expert opinion, does have a very significant impact on the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, he can't bootstrap in this document that way by the fact that he talked about it in his expert report. We've objected to his expert report on the grounds that many of the subjects he talks about are outside the scope of his expertise. He's been called as a police expert, not an expert on the government or the constitution or the interpretation of the laws. And now he's trying to get him to be allowed to testify as an expert on the matters that we say were not proffered as his area of expertise and where -- which it hasn't been shown he has the requisite expertise to make such a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Without anticipating the ultimate decision that the Chamber would make as to whether this witness is deemed competent to speak to matters outside of the confines of him being a "police expert," which the Chamber has already accepted, we would allow the question to be asked as Mr. Zecevic has asked it in as much as the -- as the document has, and we take Mr. Zecevic at his word, been referred to in the witness's report. But Mr. Zecevic, as I said, this is without prejudice to the ultimate decision that the Chamber will take as to whether we will accept that portion of the witness's purported expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand that, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Just for the record, it's paragraph 222 of the expert report where he is dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you have a third observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was just going to ask if I could have a reference, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I had put a question to you, you started answering. Could you please continue your answer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the conclusions of this joint session of the Presidency and government is as stated in this paragraph, that it is indispensable to centralise authority as much as possible. I believe that it refers to the Serb Republic of BH, and I link that to the decision of the 10th of June and the establishment of war commissions and war commissioners vis-à-vis each and every municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I have a further objection regarding this now upon reviewing the transcript. At page 17, line 23, Mr. Zecevic said: "Mr. Bajagic, this is another document that's not referred to in the footnotes of your report, but I have most certainly shown it to you during your proofing ..." If he's shown it to him in his proofing and it's not in his report, it should have been in his proofing note that he gave to us, and he didn't. That's another reason I object to using this document with this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I provided the proofing note, and I can probably read where I said that among others, witness will be able to comment on a number of documents which are not a part of his footnote. And then Mr. Hannis asked me what documents do I have in mind on our 65 ter list or the announced documents, and I specifically said announced document, announced documents. That the witness can comment on the announced documents. And this is announced document, as you know, it's tab number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you give us your comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Judge Hall said just a moment ago, at page 21, line 10: "Without anticipating the ultimate decision the Chamber would make about whether this witness is deemed competent ... we would allow the question to be asked as Mr. Zecevic has asked it in as much as the document has, and we take Mr. Zecevic at his word, been referred to in the witness's report." The document has not been referred to in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hannis, Mr. Zecevic never said that. He said he referred to the situation. But it is confusing, I admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move on, Mr. Zecevic. We -- obviously the number of things that Mr. Hannis has flagged means that you must move carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one question: Do you have any comment on the last sentence of this paragraph on page 5?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A conclusion was to reconsider the position of the Serbian autonomous region and the necessity for certain changes to the constitutional system of the Serb Republic of BH. I know that as a result an initiative was launched and finally new amendments were adopted to the Constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say amendments to the Constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you please look at document 44, your footnote 236.2 in conjunction with paragraph 223. That's document L86. Sir, is this the Official Gazette that contains the amendments that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These amendments were published in this particular Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The amendments are dated what, according to this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to promulgate these amendments was adopted by the Assembly of the Republika Srpska on the 14th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The previous document, can you remember which date it had? And I'm referring to the minutes of the joint session of the government and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was 10th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that was the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said 10th of July. Can you please look again at document tab 12, 474D1.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the 1st of July. But you called up a number of documents from July and that is the reason why I made this mistake. So it was the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you -- but let me ask you this first: Do you know if a state organ in May of 1992 requested the Crisis Staffs to be abolished?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in the course of the analysis of the document I had an opportunity to see something to that effect, but I don't remember exactly which state organ was in question. I'm sure I saw that kind of initiative, but I cannot remember any details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the Government of the Republika Srpska was that body, would that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection. That's leading. The witness says he can't remember which, and now he's telling him which one it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hannis, I am trying to refresh the witness's memory. This document is anyway already in evidence. Therefore, there is no dispute whatsoever. And we already commented on it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, bearing in mind your expert report, specifically paragraphs 220, 221, 222, 223, 228, can you give us a kind of summary of your opinion that would help us to understand what kind of standpoint you took in these specific paragraphs? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever since the promulgation of the constitution in March of 1992 until the aforementioned constitutional amendment already had within its system autonomous regions and Serbian autonomous district. In view of the situation on the ground in the first half of the year, at least up until July, we can see that the central organ of authority in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had difficulties to operate in compliance with the law and the constitution. The original constitution stipulates that the territory of the Serbian republic was unified, but it is said in the law that these autonomous region districts would be recognised within the first six months of the functioning of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please slow down because obviously you're not understood properly. When you said that the autonomous regions in compliance with the constitutional law were to be recognised or, I don't know which specific term you used, can you please say what you specifically had in mind? And can you please speak slowly in order to allow the interpreters to interpret everything that you say.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the rules and regulations were designed with the aim to have, as of September 1992, the Serbian autonomous region and the Serbian autonomous districts on the course of abolishment. So from September 1992, the legal system of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not recognise any longer the Serbian autonomous regions and autonomous districts. I think that would be the crux of the matter and my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you wanted to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, while I was perusing the binder that I have in front of me, I just tore a piece of paper, and I just wanted to glue it before we start the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is the headphone situation a bit better now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only hear you as you speak but not through the earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You'll be assisted. Can you hear me now? We are close enough to speak as we are, but is it fine now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you through the earphones now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, subparagraph 3 bears the headline of your expert report MUP in times of an imminent threat of war and war. Specifically 239, paragraph 239, details the legal provisions and regulations which I suppose you thought were important. Can you please comment on the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day of my testimony, I spoke of the relevant legal provisions important for the workings of all the state agencies in the Serbian Republic of BH, and I mentioned a whole variety of legislation including the constitution as well as some bylaws and laws which were adopted at the time of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As I state in paragraph 239 of my expert report, these include the Law on the All People's Defence of the SFRY, the rules of the army of the SFRY in part, and the strategy of the All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection. The Constitution of the SRBH as well as all the system-related laws which were taken on for the purposes of Republika Srpska envisaged that in addition to this legislation, also in force would be the laws of the SFRY, if necessary, and where these are not contrary to the Constitution of the SRBH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record I want to indicate the Prosecution's ongoing objection to this witness, who's a police expert, testifying about these matters which appear to relate to the constitution, the Law on All People's Defence, and other matters which we say are beyond his area of expertise. There's nothing to indicate in his CV or his work history that, I haven't even seen, he did his mandatory military service. So we say this is subject matter outside the scope of his expertise and would like to have on the record our continuing objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please. For the record, Mr. Hannis's objection is noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can we have your comment on paragraph 253 of your report and footnote 275. In other words, paragraphs 252, 253, and footnote 275. If we can have your brief comments on these.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that the Law on the All People's Defence of the SFRY and the strategy of ONO and DSZ were in force within the legal framework of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was able to engage in certain activities in accordance with these laws. In paragraph 252 of my report, I invoked an order issued by the minister of the interior wherein he, in keeping with the laws in force and the decision of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, declaring a state of an imminent threat of war in the Serbian republic, ordered that all the authorised officials of the Ministry of the Interior should be organised into war units for the purposes of defending the areas of the Serbian Republic of the BH. Furthermore, in paragraph 253, I go on to analyse the order, and what I highlight in particular is item 3 of that order, which reads: "In conducting combat activities, the units of the Ministry of the Interior shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces, but the units of the ministry shall be under the direct command of employees or members of the ministry." As we can see, these two paragraphs deal with this general statement of mine and with the order issued by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could make an intervention in the transcript. At page 29, line 3, it says: "In conducting combat activities, the units of the Ministry ... shall be subordinated ..." I note in the report, the English translation, at paragraph 253 at page 95, translates it as: "While carrying out combat operations." So it's important to the Prosecution if we can have a clarification from CLSS either now from the interpreters in the booth or officially in writing later on as to whether or not the term in Serbian means combat activities or combat operations, because it may become important later on to know which it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the appropriate request would be made. But I confess, Mr. Hannis, that but for your intervention, I would have myself considered the terms as interchangeable. But you may have an argument, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in order to assist the Honourable Chamber and my learned friend Mr. Hannis, let's have a look at the document which is behind tab 55. As we said, it's your footnote 275, and the document is 1D446. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in these two paragraphs 252 and 253 that I invoked the document you've just shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have item 7 shown, please. Item 7 and 8 of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me first put a question to you. In paragraph 253 of your paper, you say, in the third sentence - I suppose this is an error - you say in the third line of what should be item 3 of point 7, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely so. In the third sentence of item -- just as you've put it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you've commented on this paragraph in your report, and we have it there. What I'm particularly interested in is hearing your explanation of item 8, paragraphs 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 8 of the order, as we can see, addresses the performance of regular duties and activities of the Ministry of the Interior and its members, and states that the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs and other regulations in force of the Serbian republic must be strictly adhered to in the performance of these duties. So it all has to do with the performance of duties and activities of the Ministry of the Interior which fall within its purview as defined by the law; whereas, in the last and penultimate lines it is stated that in military activities, military regulations and rules should be enforced. In other words, in such situations where members of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska participate in military activities, that military rules and regulations shall be applicable to them, rather than the rules that would normally apply to them when they discharge their regular duties. In the second part of item 8 it is stated that any violation of regulations and issued orders shall be subject to severe punishment and result in appropriate disciplinary and criminal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have your comments on paragraph 255 of your report in connection with what you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 255, which relates to a number of paragraphs that I've already discussed based on the order we've just discussed and the laws in effect, I concluded that members of the Ministry of the Interior in the relevant period which took part in combat activities together with the army had to be subordinated to the relevant senior officer or command in the territory where the combat activities were carried out. Of course, what I also analyse here is the fact that it is said that they would be under direct command of an official of the Ministry of the Interior. Now, the fact that officials of the Ministry of the Interior were duty-bound to act in an organised fashion, duty-bound by the laws in effect, regardless of the tasks placed before them, and that somebody had to take them to the command to which they were being re-subordinated. Up until the moment when a unit of the Ministry of the Interior arrived within the area of responsibility where military activities were carried out with their respective superior and until such time as they report to the commanding officer in that area, from that point on they are all re-subordinated to the military command and from that moment they become conscripts, rather than officials or members, of the Ministry of the Interior. In other words, for as long as they are being re-subordinated, they are treated as conscripts and must abide by all the valid military laws and regulations. And it is in that sense that a broad explanation was provided on the issue in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the point in time when members of the MUP are re-subordinated to the army and for the duration of their re-subordination, do they -- are they divested of the powers that they normally have as authorised officials?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment they are re-subordinated up until the moment they return to their home MUP units, in other words, during that time they are re-subordinated to the military command, in that period of time they do not have the capacity of authorised officials; rather, they are under the command of military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they are not there in the capacity of authorised officials. For the duration of their re-subordination, they also do not have the obligations and duties that they normally have whilst working within the Ministry of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this conclusion could be drawn from my earlier comments. They do not have the obligations and duties that they have when discharging peacetime activities. So, number one, they don't have the duties and obligations that arise from the remit of the Ministry of the Interior; and, second, they do not have these inherent duties and obligations to perform them. And this clearly follows from the order that I referred to in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will have to repeat your answer because it's quite unclear because of course they could not follow what you were saying. So, while they are re-subordinated, do the members of the MUP have duties and powers that belong to them on the basis of their work, I mean, in their capacity of employees of Ministry of the Interior and that belong to them on the basis of the Law on Internal Affairs? Just answer slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior do not have these powers, duties, and responsibilities on the basis of the Law on Internal Affairs in all situations when they are subordinated to a military command. So then the Law on Internal Affairs does not apply to them; rather, it is only legal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say legal regulations. What regulations do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I most certainly mean the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army, and other legal documents that are in force in the military system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You meant military legal regulations; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those that regulate that entire subject matter that has to do with members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us try to illustrate this so that we would be done with explaining this issue once and for all. And it's a rather controversial issue. Members of the Ministry of the Interior, while they are re-subordinated to the military, do they have the authority to detain, arrest, a person?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior, while they are subordinated, do not have the authority to take such measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior, when they carry out their regular tasks in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs, do they have such authority then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When members of the Ministry of the Interior carry out their regular tasks which belong to the purview of the Ministry of the Interior, then, among other powers, they have the powers that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When they exercise these regular powers and authority that they have - I think that you have already spoken about this, but please remind us once again: Do they have the right to use force, including in some cases the use of fire-arms, in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like members of any police force in the world, the members of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska in that period of time and in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs had the right, according to law, to use an entire set of such instruments of force, that is to say when all legal requirements are met, including the right to use fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with their regular duties and responsibilities and powers in line with the Law on Internal Affairs, do members of the Ministry of the Interior have the duty and obligation to go after a perpetrator of a crime once they have learned of the commission of that crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. One of the duties of the Ministry of the Interior is to prevent and control all forms of crime, so they have that duty as well, to pursue persons who commit crimes and ultimately bring them to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If such a member of the Ministry of the Interior, with all these powers that you have explained to us just now that he or she has within his own regular duties, rights, and responsibilities, is re-subordinated to the army, and while he is re-subordinated to the army he sees that a crime is being committed, is it the duty of that individual to act then in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs and the powers vested in him on the basis of that law or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a member of the Ministry of the Interior does not have the right to exercise the powers that are derived from the Law on Internal Affairs. He is then re-subordinated. And therefore while he is re-subordinated he has lost these powers and does not have the right to apply them in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From that point of view, a member of the ministry who is re-subordinated to the army and while he is re-subordinated to the army, while combat operations are underway, in your view is he fully equal to other members of the military and the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is fully equal to all military conscripts, or, rather, members of the armed forces, in terms of rights and responsibilities and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to this document just briefly, the one that's in front of us. That is your tab 55. I hope you still have it in front of you. We have commented upon paragraphs 7 and 8; please bear that in mind because of my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown tab 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is your footnote 187.2 [as interpreted], otherwise it is document L, number 1. L001, rather. That is the Law on All People's Defence. I would like to have a look at Article 104, subparagraphs 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It we could have it on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I confirm: The transcript says footnote 187.2. I don't see a reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that the English translation that we see is not appropriate. This is the translation of some other law into English. I'll give you the ERN number of that document that I have in Serbian. 0046-1906. The Serbian version is right. Yes, yes. That's the right translation, but we now see Article 106 and we actually need 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago we looked at this order that you referred to in your footnote 275 in relation to your paragraphs 252, 253, and onwards. As we said, it has to do with point 7. Tell me, in your opinion is this order in correlation with Article 104 of the Law on All People's Defence that we see before us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that in the legal system of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Law on All People's Defence of the SFRY was in force. This is not only in correlation. As a matter of fact, the order that I referred to in that footnote is directly related to Article 104 which says that in war time, in times of imminent threat of war and in other emergencies, the police may be used for carrying out combat activities for the armed forces in accordance with the law. Also, the other part of the order is directly related to subparagraph 2, where it says: "During its engagement for combat activities in the armed forces, the police shall be re-subordinated to the officer in charge of the combat activity." That is to say, the unit that that military officer commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While we still have this law in front of us, I would like to ask you to comment on Article 105 and your paragraph 248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we come to that, I would like to ask -- I would like to ask the expert the following: You said, Mr. Bajagic, when re-subordinated, the police officer stops to be an official -- an authorised official. Stops to be a police officer basically; right? Being an official -- an authorised official is an official capacity, and I suppose that the police officer has to know exactly when this official capacity of his stops and when it starts again. So my question is: How does that happen? How does the police officer know that now he is not a police officer anymore, or he has not the capacities of such a position? And how -- and what tells him that as from this moment on he is again a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give a somewhat broader illustration. A unit of the Ministry of the Interior gets an order to travel, if it's a case of travel, and to report to a military officer. From that moment onwards, they are subordinated to him. The officer who was in charge of the unit that will be re-subordinated in its entirety will probably inform every member of the ministry, and as authorised officials they probably learn of that beforehand. They have to learn of all situations when they can exercise their authority and their powers. When a person is first employed with the Ministry of the Interior, he or she becomes familiar with their rights and responsibilities. So every member of the Ministry of the Interior as soon as he arrives and as soon as his immediate officer re-subordinates himself and his entire unit to a military officer, then the said person knows that he does not have the rights and responsibilities that he had under the Law on Internal Affairs until they go back to that organisational unit from where they had left when they became re-subordinated to a particular military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I asked you to comment on paragraph 248 of your report, of your research, in connection with Article 105 of the Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was analysing the strategy of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection and in connection with the Law on All People's Defence, as I stated in paragraph 248, I observed an interesting fact. Let me just state before that the two laws implied that the armed forces of the SFRY at the time were constituted by the army and the Territorial Defence. The interesting fact that I observed, and which is defined also by Article 105 of the Law on People's Defence, is that in the event of an imminent threat of war and in other emergencies, the duties of maintaining public law and order as well as other activities pertaining to the field of social self-protection may also be performed by the Territorial Defence. Therefore, under the law, the Territorial Defence is empowered to carry out some specific tasks in such circumstances which would normally, in peacetime, be carried out by the Ministry of the Interior. I hope that my explanation was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before you move on, if I could have a clarification. The transcript says it was a comment on paragraph 248 in connection with Article 105, and in English my paragraph 248 is talking about the strategy of the ONO. Is that correct? So it's the strategy on All People's Defence as opposed to the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain the relationship between the Law on All People's Defence and the strategy of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the strategy of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection is fully within the spirit and meaning of the Law on All People's Defence. Article 105 of the law regulates the matters that I've just referred to, which matters are repeated at page 58 of the document entitled, "Strategy of All People's Defence." In other words, the strategy paper has merely reiterated the norms and constructs put in place by the Law on the All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be the right moment to go back to an issue or, rather, a document, and we'd like to have your comments on it. It's tab 21. The document number is 1D257. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a dispatch from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 8th of April, 1992, signed by O. Jasarevic. It is addressed to all and related to the dispatch from the Ministry of National Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 5th of April. Can you comment on the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document also defines the issue of subordination in general terms. However, in relation to the Law on the All People's Defence and strategy, it is quite the inverse, quite the opposite, because the law states that police units are to be subordinated to military officers; whereas this particular document places it quite in the inverse, that all the forces should be subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior, and it's referring to the public security stations. Not only they, but all those who have anything do with the ministry in any way, including the category of volunteers and other conscripts. In other words, the order such as this one is in violation of all the legal provisions, because none of the laws envisage that any forces may be subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior; rather, it is quite the opposite, that the members of the MUP and the MUP itself may be subordinated to armed forces. In my view, this is quite a surprising document. The conclusion that I can draw from this is that, generally speaking, the Ministry of the Interior, the central authority in Sarajevo, because we are talking about the 8th of April, is used to make armed forces. So the armed forces are made out of the Ministry of the Interior. That's the conclusion that I can draw on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions on this. Sir, we were able to see the relevant legal provisions that you mentioned in your report and among them was the Law on the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If I'm not mistaken, yesterday we analysed the Law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 and the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska or Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1992. In your view, does the Law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning the issue of Internal Affairs contain any sort of legal basis that would provide the order such as this one that we have before us legality?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is not an assumption. I'm quite certain that the Law on Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 did not envisage situations such as this one and did not confer any powers for this course of action to be taken. In that context, this specific order is completely unlawful in terms of this particular law and all the other legislation that was in force in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any knowledge about the work -- or, rather, do you have any knowledge arising from the research that you made for this report that in the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there were cases where, quite inversely, as you put it, armed formations were subordinated to the police? Do you know of any such cases? And if you do, tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. In the first part of my expert report, there was a dispatch from the SJB Bratunac which was cited in this expert report which I compared with the situation in Croatia, in the Republic of Croatia, in 1990 and 1991. As I was reviewing a multitude of documents for the purposes of this report and in general as I was researching contemporary security systems in Europe and worldwide, I know that the National Guards Corps, as an armed formation, emerged outside of the legal framework of the Republic of Croatia and yet became part of the organisational structure of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia as the security system in Croatia was being set up on its recognition of independence internationally. So it became part of the Ministry of the Interior as a force that was created completely outside of it, and this was a gradual process within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go back to tab 40; 178.2 is the footnote, and it's document L001. The Law on All People's Defence. Articles 104, 105. I'd like you to help us if you can, Mr. Bajagic, to explain paragraph 2 of Article 104, which reads -- in particular what I'd like you to specify is the authorised official in charge of combat activity. I know that this is outside the scope of your expertise, but perhaps you can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, having heard that concession, I want to put on the record my objection to having him comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I'll show you document 23, which is 1D406.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Document 23, tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 1st July, 1992, which is entitled, "Determination of Areas of Responsibility Order." It's signed by General Momir Talic. I'm interested in the reference to the police in the penultimate paragraph. Can we have your comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps says that in carrying out combat activities, all the police special forces shall be placed under the command of the commander of the area who will decide on how to employ them or engage them. So this is part and parcel of the order and is fully consistent with the other documents that we looked at, namely the Law on All People's Defence and the strategy of ONO and DSZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown document 14. 65 ter -- or, rather, 1D409. I think it's been MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what we see here is coming from the command of the 1st Battalion of the Serbian army, Osmaci, the 5th of November, 1992. It's an order signed by commander Bosko Djuricic. It reads that: "Due to the serious situation on the front line, until further notice the Osmaci civilian police will not perform duties at the check-point or any other type of assignments except at a front line position." Based on what I have just read to you, can you draw any collusion whatsoever as to whether here we have a case of re-subordination of the police to the army in line with the rules and regulations that we had just seen a minute ago or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see in this document once again that the civilian police, i.e., members of the ministry, are being placed under the command of a platoon commander probably in order to be engaged in combat assignments. So basically we are facing here a case of re-subordination and they are given a totally different set of tasks under the platoon commander's direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to a different subject. Sir, paragraph 312, I believe we mentioned it earlier. 312, 314, and 316.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So from paragraph 312 onwards through a number of the paragraphs that follow, I addressed the issue of certain provisions of the internal organisation of the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of B&H from 1990, which in the course of 1992 was in force and applied to the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH. In a number of paragraphs, I specifically dealt with the area relating to the tasks of road safety. And having analysed the set of rules from 1990, I realised that from the top of the ministry all the way down to the very bottom, that is to say, SJB via CSB, there were specific organisational units that were in charge of planning, organisation, and implementation of the tasks that have to do with road safety in the broadest of terms. So I recognised that within security services centres there were special police stations dedicated to road safety, and this set of rules says that at the level of the public security service, as one of the main ministry departments, there was a separate section dedicated to road safety. This is what I commented on in the paragraphs mentioned above.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in your opinion, concerning these members of the Ministry of the Interior who were involved in very specific tasks such as road safety and similar, were the rules on re-subordination applied to them as well in line with the law and pursuant to the order issued on the 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, provided they find themselves in a situation in which they have to carry tasks in a co-ordinated action, and within the system of re-subordination, to a military unit.
